about:
Reference pages for the AI syllabus, one per topic (topic 0 is prior learning), shown on the Syllabus tab for AI SL and AI HL. Same HTML dialect as data/syllabus-docs-aa.json: one

code title

section per statement in data/syllabus-ai.json, with .formula and .formula-inline elements rendered by KaTeX. Formulas follow the AI formula booklet; sections for statements shared with AA repeat the AA page. The page shows each course only its own statements and marks the additional higher level ones itself.

topics.title: Prior learning
topics.html:
Prior Learning

Area

Plane shapes

A_{\text{parallelogram}}=bh
A_{\text{triangle}}=\frac{1}{2}bh
A_{\text{trapezoid}}=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h
A_{\text{circle}}=\pi r^2

Circumference of a circle

C=2\pi r

Curved surface of a cylinder

A=2\pi rh

Volume

V_{\text{cuboid}}=lwh
V_{\text{cylinder}}=\pi r^2h
V_{\text{prism}}=Ah
  • A is the area of the cross-section of the prism and h its height.

Coordinate geometry

Distance between two points (x_1,y_1) and (x_2,y_2)

d=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}

Midpoint of a line segment

\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)

topics.title: Number and Algebra
topics.html:
Topic 1: Number and Algebra

1.1 Scientific notation

  • Operations with numbers in the form a \times 10^k, where 1 \le a < 10 and k is an integer.
  • Calculator notation is not accepted as final scientific notation.

1.2 Arithmetic sequences and series

nth term

u_n = u_1 + (n-1)d

Sum of the first n terms

S_n = \frac{n}{2}(2u_1 + (n-1)d)

or

S_n = \frac{n}{2}(u_1 + u_n)

Sigma notation

\sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i

1.3 Geometric sequences and series

nth term

u_n = u_1 r^{n-1}

Sum of the first n terms

S_n = \frac{u_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}, \quad r \ne 1

1.4 Financial applications of geometric sequences and series

Compound interest

FV = PV\left(1+\frac{r}{100k}\right)^{kn}

Where:

  • PV = present value
  • FV = future value
  • r = annual interest rate (%)
  • k = compounding periods per year
  • n = number of years
  • Includes annual depreciation and other geometric financial models.

1.5 Laws of exponents with integer exponents and introduction to logarithms

Integer exponent laws

a^m a^n = a^{m+n}
\frac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}
(a^m)^n=a^{mn}
(ab)^n=a^n b^n

Definition

a^x = b \iff x = \log_a b \quad (a>0,\ a\ne1)

Natural logarithm

\ln x = \log_{\mathrm{e}} x
  • Includes base 10 and base \mathrm{e} logarithms.
  • Includes numerical evaluation of logarithms using technology.

1.6 Approximation, bounds, percentage error and estimation

Percentage error

\varepsilon=\left|\frac{v_A-v_E}{v_E}\right|\times 100\%

Where:

  • v_E = exact value
  • v_A = approximate value
  • Rounding to decimal places and significant figures, with an accuracy that suits the data and the context (for example currency).
  • Upper and lower bounds of rounded values.
  • Maximum percentage error caused by rounding a measurement.
  • Judging whether a calculated result is reasonable.

1.7 Amortization and annuities using technology

  • Loan amortization and annuity problems, solved with technology (the GDC finance solver or a spreadsheet).
  • Repayments, number of payments, interest rate, outstanding balance and total interest.
  • In examinations payments are made at the end of each period.
  • The annuity formula helps understanding but is not examined.

1.8 Solving linear systems and polynomial equations with technology

  • Systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns, solved with technology.
  • Polynomial equations solved with technology, using the terms zeros and roots.
  • No particular method is required.
  • Systems in examinations always have a unique solution.

1.9 Laws of logarithms

Laws of logarithms

\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y
\log_a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=\log_a x-\log_a y
\log_a(x^m)=m\log_a x

For a,x,y>0.

  • In examinations a=10 or a=\mathrm{e}.
  • Combining or expanding logarithmic expressions.
  • Solving equations with the laws of logarithms.

1.10 Simplifying expressions with rational exponents

Rational exponents

a^{\frac{1}{m}}=\sqrt[m]{a}
a^{\frac{m}{n}}=\sqrt[n]{a^m}
  • Simplifying numerical and algebraic expressions with the laws of exponents.
  • Includes negative fractional exponents.

1.11 Sum of infinite geometric sequences

Sum to infinity

S_\infty = \frac{u_1}{1-r}, \quad |r|<1

1.12 Complex numbers in Cartesian form

Cartesian form

z=a+b\mathrm{i},\quad \mathrm{i}^2=-1

Solutions of ax^2+bx+c=0, a\ne 0

x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}

Discriminant

\Delta=b^2-4ac
  • Real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument.
  • Sums, differences, products and quotients by hand and with technology; powers with technology.
  • The complex plane (Argand diagram).
  • A real quadratic with \Delta<0 has complex roots, and its graph does not meet the x-axis.

1.13 Polar and exponential forms of complex numbers

Polar and exponential forms

z=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r\operatorname{cis}\theta
  • Conversion between Cartesian, polar and exponential forms, by hand and with technology.
  • Products, quotients and integer powers in polar or exponential form; finding roots is not required.
  • Adding sinusoidal functions of equal frequency using complex numbers.
  • Addition seen as vector addition; multiplication as a rotation with a stretch.

1.14 Matrices: algebra, determinants, inverses and linear systems

Determinant of a 2\times 2 matrix

\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\Rightarrow\det\boldsymbol{A}=|\boldsymbol{A}|=ad-bc

Inverse of a 2\times 2 matrix

\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det\boldsymbol{A}}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix},\quad ad\ne bc
  • Element, row, column and order of a matrix.
  • Equality, addition, subtraction, multiplication by a scalar and matrix multiplication; identity and zero matrices.
  • Determinants and inverses by hand for 2\times 2 matrices and with technology for larger ones.
  • Solving \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b} with the inverse matrix, for example in coding messages; \boldsymbol{A} is always invertible in examinations.

1.15 Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalisation of 2 × 2 matrices

Power formula for a matrix

\boldsymbol{M}^n=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}^n\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}

Where:

  • \boldsymbol{P} = matrix of eigenvectors
  • \boldsymbol{D} = diagonal matrix of eigenvalues
  • Characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2\times 2 matrices, by hand and with technology.
  • Diagonalization of 2\times 2 matrices with distinct real eigenvalues.
  • Applications such as population movement between two places and predator-prey models.

topics.title: Functions
topics.html:
Topic 2: Functions

2.1 Equations of straight lines, parallel and perpendicular

Forms of a line

y = mx + c
ax + by + d = 0
y-y_1=m(x-x_1)

Gradient between two points

m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}
  • Parallel lines have equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is -1.

2.2 Functions, notation, domain, range and inverse as reflection

  • Function notation, for example f(x), v(t), C(n).
  • Domain, range and graph.
  • Informal inverse function concept.
  • Inverse function as reflection in the line y=x.

2.3 Graphs of functions

  • The graph of a function and its equation y=f(x).
  • Sketching graphs from information given or from context.
  • Using technology to graph functions, including sums and differences.

2.4 Key features of graphs

  • Maximum and minimum values.
  • Intercepts, symmetry, vertex and zeros.
  • Vertical and horizontal asymptotes.
  • Points of intersection of curves or lines using technology.

2.5 Modelling with linear, quadratic, exponential, power, cubic and sinusoidal functions

Linear

f(x)=mx+c

Quadratic

f(x)=ax^2+bx+c
\text{Axis of symmetry: } x=-\frac{b}{2a}

Exponential

f(x)=ka^x+c
f(x)=ka^{-x}+c
f(x)=k\mathrm{e}^{rx}+c

Direct and inverse variation

f(x)=ax^n,\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}

Cubic

f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d

Sinusoidal

f(x)=a\sin(bx)+d,\quad f(x)=a\cos(bx)+d
  • Linear models include piecewise linear models.
  • Quadratic models: vertex, axis of symmetry, zeros and intercepts; technology may be used for the roots.
  • Exponential models have a horizontal asymptote; for ax^n with n<0 the y-axis is an asymptote.
  • Sinusoidal models work in degrees: amplitude a, period \frac{360^\circ}{b} and principal axis y=d.
  • Converting between \sin and \cos is not required.

2.6 The modelling process: choose, fit, test and use a model

  • Choosing a suitable model and a sensible domain from the context.
  • Finding the parameters from initial conditions, given points or simultaneous equations solved with technology (up to three linear equations in three unknowns at SL).
  • Judging and justifying the choice of model.
  • Using the model to predict, knowing the risks of extrapolation.
  • Fitting by regression belongs to topic 4; non-linear regression is not required at SL.

2.7 Composite and inverse functions in context

Composite functions

(f \circ g)(x)=f(g(x))

Inverse functions

(f \circ f^{-1})(x)=(f^{-1}\circ f)(x)=x
  • Composite functions set in context.
  • Finding the inverse function f^{-1}.
  • Restricting the domain so that an inverse exists, for example to one side of the vertex of a quadratic.

2.8 Transformations of graphs

  • Translations:
y=f(x)+b,\quad y=f(x-a)
  • Reflections:
y=-f(x),\quad y=f(-x)
  • Vertical stretch:
y=pf(x)
  • Horizontal stretch:
y=f(qx)

2.9 Further models: half-life, logarithmic, sinusoidal, logistic and piecewise

Natural logarithmic models

f(x)=a+b\ln x

Sinusoidal models

f(x)=a\sin(b(x-c))+d

Logistic models

f(x)=\frac{L}{1+C\mathrm{e}^{-kx}},\quad L,k,C>0
  • Half-life from exponential models.
  • Sinusoidal models work in radians: period \frac{2\pi}{b}, with c a phase shift.
  • L is the carrying capacity of a logistic model.
  • Piecewise models, including finding a parameter that makes the pieces join.
  • Unfamiliar models may be defined in a question; the formal definition of continuity is not required.

2.10 Logarithmic scales and linearising data

  • Logarithmic scales compress very large or very small numbers onto a manageable scale.
  • Semi-log graphs: plotting \log y against x gives a straight line for an exponential relationship.
  • Log-log graphs: plotting \log y against \log x gives a straight line for a power relationship.
  • The line of best fit of the linearized data gives the parameters of the model.
  • Semi-log and log-log graphs are interpreted, not drawn or sketched.

topics.title: Geometry and Trigonometry
topics.html:
Topic 3: Geometry and Trigonometry

3.1 3D space, volume, angles, distance and midpoints

Distance between two points (x_1,y_1,z_1) and (x_2,y_2,z_2)

d=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2+(z_1-z_2)^2}

Midpoint of a line segment

\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2},\frac{z_1+z_2}{2}\right)

Volume

V_{\text{right pyramid}}=\frac{1}{3}Ah
V_{\text{right cone}}=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h
V_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3

Surface area

A_{\text{curved surface of a cone}}=\pi rl
A_{\text{sphere}}=4\pi r^2
  • A is the area of the base of the pyramid and l the slant height of the cone.
  • Distance and midpoint in three-dimensional space.
  • Volume and surface area of 3D solids, including combinations of solids.
  • Angles between intersecting lines or between a line and a plane.

3.2 2D and 3D trigonometry, sine rule, cosine rule and area

Sine rule

\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}

Cosine rule

c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C

Area of a triangle

A=\frac{1}{2}ab\sin C

3.3 Applications of trigonometry

  • Applications of right- and non-right-angled trigonometry.
  • Pythagoras' theorem in context.
  • Angles of elevation and depression.
  • Bearings.

3.4 Arc length and sector area in degrees

Arc length

l=\frac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r

Sector area

A=\frac{\theta}{360}\times \pi r^2
  • \theta is the angle measured in degrees and r the radius.
  • Radians are not used at SL.

3.5 Equations of perpendicular bisectors

  • Equation of the perpendicular bisector of a segment given its two endpoints.
  • Equation of the perpendicular bisector given the equation of the line containing the segment and its midpoint.
  • Uses midpoints, perpendicular gradients and the forms of a straight line from 2.1.

3.6 Voronoi diagrams

  • Sites, vertices, edges and cells of a Voronoi diagram; adding a new site.
  • Equation of a boundary from the coordinates of the sites.
  • Nearest site to a given point, areas of cells and nearest neighbour interpolation.
  • The "toxic waste dump" problem: the solution is at a vertex where three edges meet.
  • Perpendicular bisectors are not constructed geometrically.

3.7 Radian measure

Arc length

l=r\theta

Sector area

A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta
  • \theta is the angle measured in radians and r the radius.
  • Definition of the radian and conversion between degrees and radians.
  • Radian measures as exact multiples of \pi or as decimals.

3.8 The unit circle, the Pythagorean identity, the ambiguous case and graphical trigonometric equations

Identities

\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1
\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}
  • \cos\theta and \sin\theta defined as coordinates on the unit circle; the graphs of \sin x and \cos x.
  • Ambiguous case of the sine rule.
  • Solving trigonometric equations graphically in a finite interval.
  • Exact values are not assessed.

3.9 Matrix transformations of the plane

Reflection in the line y=(\tan\theta)x

\begin{pmatrix}\cos 2\theta&\sin 2\theta\\\sin 2\theta&-\cos 2\theta\end{pmatrix}

Horizontal stretch, scale factor k

\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}

Vertical stretch, scale factor k

\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix}

Enlargement, scale factor k, centre (0,0)

\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix}

Anticlockwise rotation of angle \theta about the origin

\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}

Clockwise rotation of angle \theta about the origin

\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}

Area of the image

\text{area of image}=|\det\boldsymbol{A}|\times\text{area of object}
  • Translations are added as a vector: transformations of the form \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}.
  • Compositions of transformations.
  • Iterated transformations, such as simple fractals.

3.10 Vectors and scalars: representation and components

Magnitude of a vector

|\boldsymbol{v}|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2},\quad \boldsymbol{v}=\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\v_3\end{pmatrix}
  • Vectors as directed line segments and in component form (column vectors or \boldsymbol{i}, \boldsymbol{j}, \boldsymbol{k}); the zero vector and -\boldsymbol{v}.
  • Sums, differences, scalar multiples and resultants, algebraically and geometrically.
  • Parallel vectors and position vectors.
  • Rescaling to a unit vector or to a vector of given magnitude.

3.11 Vector equation of a line

Vector equation of a line

\boldsymbol{r}=\boldsymbol{a}+\lambda\boldsymbol{b}

Parametric form

x=x_0+\lambda l,\quad y=y_0+\lambda m,\quad z=z_0+\lambda n
  • \boldsymbol{a} is the position vector of a point on the line and \boldsymbol{b} a direction vector.
  • Lines in two and three dimensions.

3.12 Vector kinematics

Motion with constant velocity

\boldsymbol{r}=\boldsymbol{r}_0+\boldsymbol{v}t
  • Positions and times in two and three dimensions; intersections of paths and collisions.
  • Relative position \overrightarrow{AB} and closest approach.
  • Motion with variable velocity in two dimensions, with projectile and circular motion as special cases.
  • Time shifts written with t-a.

3.13 Scalar and vector products

Scalar product

\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=v_1w_1+v_2w_2+v_3w_3
\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|\cos\theta

Angle between two vectors

\cos\theta=\frac{v_1w_1+v_2w_2+v_3w_3}{|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|}

Vector product

\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}=\begin{pmatrix}v_2w_3-v_3w_2\\v_3w_1-v_1w_3\\v_1w_2-v_2w_1\end{pmatrix}
|\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}|=|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|\sin\theta

Area of a parallelogram

A=|\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}|
  • \theta is the angle between \boldsymbol{v} and \boldsymbol{w}, which form two adjacent sides of the parallelogram.
  • Acute angle between two lines; perpendicular vectors have \boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0.
  • Direction of \boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w} by the right-hand rule; area of a triangle.
  • Components of \boldsymbol{a} parallel and perpendicular to \boldsymbol{b}.
  • Proofs and general properties are not required.

3.14 Graph theory: vertices, edges, degree and types of graph

  • Vertices, edges, adjacent vertices and adjacent edges; degree of a vertex.
  • Simple, complete and weighted graphs.
  • Directed graphs: in-degree and out-degree.
  • Connected and strongly connected graphs; subgraphs and trees.
  • Representing real structures such as maps, networks and circuits as graphs.

3.15 Adjacency matrices, walks and transition matrices for graphs

  • Adjacency matrices of graphs and directed graphs.
  • Walks: the number of walks of length k (or of length up to k) from powers of the adjacency matrix.
  • Weighted adjacency tables.
  • Transition matrices for strongly connected undirected or directed graphs, with Google PageRank as an application.

3.16 Graph algorithms: Eulerian and Hamiltonian routes, spanning trees, Chinese postman and travelling salesman

  • Walks, trails, paths, circuits and cycles.
  • Eulerian trails and circuits, and deciding whether they exist; Hamiltonian paths and cycles.
  • Minimum spanning trees by Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms, including Prim's algorithm on a matrix.
  • Chinese postman problem with up to four odd vertices.
  • Travelling salesman problem: table of least distances, upper bound by the nearest neighbour algorithm and lower bound by the deleted vertex algorithm.

topics.title: Statistics and Probability
topics.html:
Topic 4: Statistics and Probability

4.1 Concepts, reliability and sampling techniques

  • Population, sample and random sample.
  • Discrete and continuous data.
  • Reliability and sampling methods.

4.2 Histograms, cumulative frequency graphs and box plots

  • Frequency distributions.
  • Histograms.
  • Cumulative frequency graphs.
  • Median, quartiles, percentiles, range and interquartile range.
  • Box-and-whisker diagrams.

4.3 Mean, median, mode, grouped mean, standard deviation, quartiles and IQR

Grouped mean

\bar{x}=\frac{\sum f_ix_i}{\sum f_i}

Interquartile range

\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1
  • Measures of central tendency and dispersion.
  • Standard deviation and variance using technology.

4.4 Pearson's, scatter diagrams and equation of y on x

  • Linear correlation of bivariate data.
  • Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient.
  • Scatter diagrams and lines of best fit.
  • Regression line of y on x.
  • Interpreting correlation and limits of extrapolation.

4.5 Probability concepts and expected numbers

\mathrm{P}(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(U)}
\mathrm{P}(A')=1-\mathrm{P}(A)
  • Trial, outcome, sample space and event.
  • Expected number of occurrences.

4.6 Combined, mutually exclusive, conditional, independence and probability diagrams

  • Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, sample-space diagrams and tables of outcomes.
  • Combined events:
\mathrm{P}(A\cup B)=\mathrm{P}(A)+\mathrm{P}(B)-\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)
  • Conditional probability:
\mathrm{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathrm{P}(B)}
  • Independent events:
\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)=\mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B)

4.7 Discrete random variables

\mathrm{E}(X)=\sum x_i\,\mathrm{P}(X=x_i)
  • Probability distributions.
  • Expected value and fair games.

4.8 Binomial distribution

X\sim \mathrm{B}(n,p)
\mathrm{E}(X)=np
\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)

4.9 Normal distribution and calculations

  • Normal distribution and curve.
  • Normal probability calculations.
  • Inverse normal calculations where mean and standard deviation are given.

4.10 Spearman's rank correlation coefficient

  • Spearman's rank correlation coefficient r_s, found with technology.
  • Equal data values are given the average of their ranks.
  • Pearson's r measures linear association only; r_s measures any monotonic association.
  • r_s is less affected by outliers than r.
  • Deriving either coefficient is not required.

4.11 Hypothesis testing: χ² tests and the t-test

  • Null and alternative hypotheses H_0 and H_1, significance levels and p-values.
  • \chi^2 test for independence: contingency tables up to 4\times 4, degrees of freedom and critical values.
  • \chi^2 goodness of fit test, comparing observed and expected frequencies.
  • Pooled two-sample t-test for unpaired samples from normal populations, one-tailed or two-tailed.
  • In examinations \chi^2 tests are upper-tail at the 1%, 5% or 10% level, the test statistic and p-value come from technology, and expected frequencies are greater than 5.

4.12 Designing data collection; reliability and validity

  • Designing valid data collection, including surveys and questionnaires with structured, unbiased and precise questions.
  • Choosing relevant variables and data to analyse.
  • Grouping numerical data into categories for a \chi^2 test so that expected frequencies are greater than 5.
  • Reducing the degrees of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data.
  • Reliability (test-retest, parallel forms) and validity (content, criterion-related).

4.13 Non-linear regression and the coefficient of determination

  • Least squares regression curves fitted with technology: linear, quadratic, cubic, exponential, power and sine models.
  • Sum of square residuals SS_{\mathrm{res}} as a measure of fit.
  • Coefficient of determination R^2: the proportion of the variation in y explained by the model; R^2=r^2 for linear models.
  • R^2 alone is not a reliable way to choose between models.
  • The formula R^2=1-\frac{SS_{\mathrm{res}}}{SS_{\mathrm{tot}}} is not examined.

4.14 Linear combinations of random variables and unbiased estimates

Linear transformation of a single random variable

\mathrm{E}(aX+b)=a\mathrm{E}(X)+b
\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)

Linear combinations of n independent random variables X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n

\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{E}(a_1X_1\pm a_2X_2\pm\dots\pm a_nX_n)\\&=a_1\mathrm{E}(X_1)\pm a_2\mathrm{E}(X_2)\pm\dots\pm a_n\mathrm{E}(X_n)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{Var}(a_1X_1\pm a_2X_2\pm\dots\pm a_nX_n)\\&=a_1^2\mathrm{Var}(X_1)+a_2^2\mathrm{Var}(X_2)+\dots+a_n^2\mathrm{Var}(X_n)\end{aligned}

Unbiased estimate of the population variance

s_{n-1}^2=\frac{n}{n-1}\,s_n^2
  • The expectation formula holds for any random variables; the variance formula needs them to be independent.
  • \bar{x} is an unbiased estimate of \mu and s_{n-1}^2 is an unbiased estimate of \sigma^2.
  • Proofs that these estimates are unbiased are not examined.

4.15 Combining normal variables and the central limit theorem

Distribution of the sample mean

X\sim \mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\Rightarrow\bar{X}\sim \mathrm{N}\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
  • A linear combination of independent normal random variables is normally distributed.
  • Central limit theorem: for large samples from any distribution the sample mean is approximately normal.
  • In examinations n>30 is large enough.

4.16 Confidence intervals for a mean

  • Confidence intervals for the mean of a normal population.
  • Use the normal distribution when \sigma is known.
  • Use the t-distribution when \sigma is unknown, whatever the sample size.
  • Interpreting the interval in context.

4.17 The Poisson distribution

X\sim \mathrm{Po}(m)
\mathrm{E}(X)=m
\mathrm{Var}(X)=m
  • Models independent events that occur at a uniform average rate.
  • The sum of two independent Poisson variables has a Poisson distribution.
  • Choosing between normal, binomial and Poisson models in context.
  • Proofs of the mean and the variance are not required.

4.18 Critical regions, tests for a mean, a proportion or a correlation, and type I and II errors

  • Critical values and critical regions.
  • Test for a population mean: the z-test when \sigma is known and the t-test when \sigma is unknown; matched pairs are treated as one sample of differences.
  • One-tailed tests for a proportion (binomial distribution) and for a mean (Poisson distribution).
  • Test for the population correlation coefficient \rho=0, with technology.
  • Type I and type II errors and their probabilities, for normal (known variance), binomial and Poisson tests.
  • Critical regions for t-tests are not required; for discrete tests the critical region is the largest one with probability below the significance level.

4.19 Transition matrices and Markov chains

Transition matrices

\boldsymbol{T}^n\boldsymbol{s}_0=\boldsymbol{s}_n
  • \boldsymbol{s}_0 is the initial state and T_{ij} the probability of moving from state j to state i.
  • Transition diagrams and transition matrices; regular Markov chains.
  • Steady state and long-term probabilities, from high powers of \boldsymbol{T} or by solving a system of linear equations.
  • The steady state as the eigenvector for the eigenvalue 1.

topics.title: Calculus
topics.html:
Topic 5: Calculus

5.1 Introduction to calculus

  • Limits from a table or graph.
  • Derivative interpreted as a gradient function and as a rate of change.
  • Notation including \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}, f'(x) and related contextual notation.

5.2 Increasing and decreasing functions

  • Graphical interpretation of f'(x)>0, f'(x)=0 and f'(x)<0.
  • Intervals of increase and decrease.

5.3 Differentiating polynomials, n in Z

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(ax^n)=anx^{n-1}, \quad n\in\mathbb{Z}
  • Differentiating sums and multiples of polynomial terms with integer exponents.

5.4 Tangents and normals

  • Tangents and normals at a given point.
  • Equations of tangents and normals.

5.5 Integration introduction, areas between curve and x-axis

Integral of x^n

\int x^n\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C \quad (n\ne -1)

Area between a curve y=f(x) and the x-axis, where f(x)>0

A=\int_a^b y\,\mathrm{d}x
  • Integration as anti-differentiation for polynomial functions with integer exponents.
  • Anti-differentiation with boundary conditions.
  • Definite integrals using technology.
  • Area under a curve where f(x)>0.

5.6 Stationary points: local maxima and minima

  • Points of zero gradient, found by solving f'(x)=0.
  • Technology may be used to find f'(x) and to solve the equation.
  • Local maximum and minimum points.
  • A local maximum or minimum is not necessarily the greatest or least value of the function on its domain.
  • The second derivative test is not required at SL.

5.7 Optimisation in context

  • Optimisation problems in context, solved with calculus and technology.
  • Maximising profit or volume; minimising cost or material.
  • Setting up the function from a constraint, such as a fixed volume or surface area.
  • Kinematics optimisation is not set at SL.

5.8 Approximating areas with the trapezoidal rule

The trapezoidal rule

\begin{aligned}\int_a^b y\,\mathrm{d}x\approx\frac{1}{2}h\bigl(&(y_0+y_n)\\&+2(y_1+y_2+\dots+y_{n-1})\bigr)\end{aligned}
h=\frac{b-a}{n}
  • Uses n intervals of equal width h.
  • Given a function or a table of data, such as measurements of an irregular shape.
  • Comparing the estimate with the true value: overestimate or underestimate.

5.9 Further differentiation: standard derivatives, chain, product and quotient rules, related rates

Standard derivatives

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}, \quad n\in\mathbb{Q}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\sin x)=\cos x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\cos x)=-\sin x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\tan x)=\frac{1}{\cos^2 x}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\mathrm{e}^x)=\mathrm{e}^x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\ln x)=\frac{1}{x}

Chain rule

\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}

Product rule

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(uv)=u\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}

Quotient rule

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)=\frac{v\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}-u\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}}{v^2}
  • Related rates of change.
  • Stationary points and optimisation with these functions (see 5.6 and 5.7).

5.10 The second derivative and the second derivative test

  • Second derivative notation including \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} and f''(x).
  • Second derivative test for local maximum and minimum points.
  • Concave-up where f''(x)>0 and concave-down where f''(x)<0.
  • Points of inflexion, where the concavity changes, interpreted in context.

5.11 Further integration: standard integrals, inspection and substitution

Standard integrals

\int x^n\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C \quad (n\ne -1)
\int \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=\ln|x|+C
\int \sin x\,\mathrm{d}x=-\cos x+C
\int \cos x\,\mathrm{d}x=\sin x+C
\int \frac{1}{\cos^2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x=\tan x+C
\int \mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x=\mathrm{e}^x+C
  • Definite and indefinite integrals, with n\in\mathbb{Q}.
  • Integration by inspection or by the substitution u=g(x) for integrals of the form \int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.
  • Includes composites with linear functions, such as \sin(2x+5).

5.12 Areas against either axis and volumes of revolution

Area of a region enclosed by a curve and the x-axis or y-axis

A=\int_a^b y\,\mathrm{d}x \quad\text{or}\quad A=\int_a^b x\,\mathrm{d}y

Volume of revolution about the x-axis or y-axis

V=\int_a^b \pi y^2\,\mathrm{d}x \quad\text{or}\quad V=\int_a^b \pi x^2\,\mathrm{d}y
  • Regions in a given interval, including parts below the axis, where the integral is negative.

5.13 Kinematics problems

v=\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t}
a=\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}^2s}{\mathrm{d}t^2}
\text{displacement}=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
\text{distance}=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}|v(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t

5.14 Setting up differential equations and separating variables

Exponential model

\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=ky \Rightarrow y=A\mathrm{e}^{kx}
  • Forming a differential equation from a description in context, such as a rate proportional to the amount present.
  • Solving by separation of variables.
  • General solution, with an arbitrary constant, and particular solutions from given conditions.

5.15 Slope fields

\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=f(x,y)
  • Slope fields drawn as short segments with the gradient at each grid point.
  • Matching slope fields to differential equations.
  • Sketching the solution curve through a given point.
  • Reading features such as equilibrium solutions and long-term behaviour.

5.16 Euler's method for single and coupled first-order equations

Euler's method

y_{n+1}=y_n+h\times f(x_n,y_n),\quad x_{n+1}=x_n+h

Euler's method for coupled systems

x_{n+1}=x_n+h\times f_1(x_n,y_n,t_n)
y_{n+1}=y_n+h\times f_2(x_n,y_n,t_n)
t_{n+1}=t_n+h
  • h is a constant (the step length).
  • Approximate solutions of \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=f(x,y) and of coupled systems \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=f_1(x,y,t), \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=f_2(x,y,t), such as predator-prey models.
  • Values are generated with a spreadsheet or the GDC.
  • Understanding the step-by-step method, the effect of the step length and how to interpret the output.

5.17 Phase portraits for coupled linear differential equations

Coupled linear system

\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=ax+by,\quad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=cx+dy

Exact solution

\boldsymbol{x}=A\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_1t}\boldsymbol{p}_1+B\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_2t}\boldsymbol{p}_2
  • \lambda_1,\lambda_2 are the eigenvalues and \boldsymbol{p}_1,\boldsymbol{p}_2 the corresponding eigenvectors; the eigenvalues are distinct and non-zero.
  • Phase portraits: classifying the origin from the eigenvalues (real, complex or purely imaginary).
  • Sketching trajectories; equilibrium points, stability and saddle points.
  • Exact solutions are required only for real distinct eigenvalues.

5.18 Second-order differential equations by Euler's method

Second-order equation

\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=f\left(x,\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t},t\right)

Written as a coupled system

\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=y,\quad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=f(x,y,t)
  • Approximate solutions by applying Euler's method to the coupled system.
  • Equations of the form \frac{\mathrm{d}^2x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+a\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}+bx=0 can also be studied with the phase portraits of 5.17.
  • The equation is always given in examinations.
